title: Preach the Word
subtitle: The Primacy of Expository Preaching in the Local Church
blurb: The pulpit has become a stage, and the sermon a performance measured by how well it moves a room. This book argues that the preacher's only authority is the text in front of him, that exposition is not a method among methods but the recovery of a church that has stopped expecting God to speak. It is written for the pastor who is tired of being interesting and wants, again, to be faithful.

chapters.title: The Command Beneath the Office
chapters.summary: Paul's charge to Timothy is not advice but an order given under the weight of God and the coming judgment. To preach the word is to obey a command, not to express a gift.
chapters.body:
There is a sentence in the New Testament that should have ended the career of every man who ever stood behind a pulpit to be admired. Paul is in prison. He is going to die, and he knows it, and the next words he writes are not soft. "I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom; Preach the word" (2 Timothy 4:1-2). Read it again and notice what it is not. It is not encouragement. It is not a suggestion offered to a younger man with promise. It is a charge laid before the judgment seat, sworn under the name of the God who will sort the living from the dead, and the verb at the center of it is an imperative.

Preach. Herald. Announce what you have been given to announce.

I came to faith out of atheism, and one of the things the church never quite prepared me for was how quickly the sacred can be domesticated by the people who handle it most. I was handed a microphone before I understood what the microphone was for. I assumed, the way most of us assume, that the sermon was the place where I demonstrated that I had something to say. That assumption is the original corruption of the pulpit, and it is so common we have stopped naming it as corruption at all. We call it style. We call it voice. We call it knowing your gifts. Paul calls it nothing. Paul does not ask Timothy whether he has anything to say. Paul tells him what to say, and the thing to say is not his.

This is the first wall every preacher hits, and most of us spend a decade pretending it is not there. The word is not yours. You did not write it, you cannot improve it, and on the days you find it dull, the dullness is in you and not in it. The office of preaching is not the platform for a man's insight. It is the conscript service of a herald who carries a message he did not compose and may not edit. John Stott, in *Between Two Worlds*, called the preacher a bridge between the ancient text and the modern world, and the image is useful as far as it goes, but a bridge does not get to decide where the road leads. It only spans the distance. The traffic is not its own.

Consider the setting of Paul's charge, because the setting is the argument. He invokes God. He invokes Christ as judge. He invokes the appearing and the kingdom. He stacks four eschatological realities on top of one another before he ever reaches the verb, and the effect is to crush every smaller motive a preacher might bring to the task. You cannot stand under that sentence and still be primarily interested in whether the congregation found you compelling. The judgment of the room is swallowed by the judgment of the throne. Spurgeon, who knew more about holding a crowd than any of us, said he trembled lest he should preach himself and not Christ, and that trembling was not false modesty. It was the only sane response to the charge. A man who does not tremble has not understood what he is holding.

I have watched the office decay in slow motion across my own ministry, and the decay rarely announces itself. It does not begin with a pastor deciding to abandon Scripture. It begins with a pastor deciding that Scripture needs his help to be heard. He starts with the text and then drifts toward the illustration that lands better than the text did. He notices which sentences earn the nods and which earn the silence, and being human, being a man who wants to be useful, he leans toward the nods. Within a few years the text has become the pretext, a verse read at the top to bless a talk that would have existed without it. The congregation does not notice the substitution because the substitution feels like care. It feels like relevance. It is theft, and it is theft we have learned to praise.

Martyn Lloyd-Jones, in *Preaching and Preachers*, refused to let the matter rest on technique. He insisted that preaching is theology coming through a man who is on fire, and that the great need of the church was not better methods but men who had been mastered by the truth before they presumed to deliver it. I think he was right, and I think his diagnosis cuts against the grain of everything our era rewards. We reward the man who has mastered the room. Scripture commissions the man who has been mastered by the word. Those are not the same man, and the distance between them is the distance between a performer and a herald.

So what does it mean, concretely, to obey the charge rather than fill the office? It means the text sets the agenda before I do. It means that when I open the passage on Monday I am not asking what I want to say this week but what this passage says, and I am binding myself to that answer even when it is inconvenient, even when it preaches against me, even when it will not flatter the people I most want to flatter. It means I preach what is there. Not what I wish were there. Not what the moment seems to demand. What is there.

Augustine understood this fifteen hundred years before any of our anxieties about relevance. In the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine* he turned to the question of Christian eloquence and concluded that the preacher's eloquence must serve the truth and never the reverse, that a wise man speaking obscurely is better than a fool speaking beautifully, and that the highest skill is the skill that disappears so the matter can be seen. He did not despise rhetoric. He had taught it for a living. But he subordinated it, completely and without apology, to the thing being said. That subordination is the whole ballgame. The moment the saying becomes more important than the said, you have left the office of herald and entered the trade of entertainer, and you will be paid accordingly, in the currency of applause that means nothing on the day Paul described.

I am inside this indictment. I have preached myself. I have stood up with a text I had not loved enough to obey and dressed it in a delivery I had practiced more than I had prayed over. I know the particular guilt of watching a room respond to a sentence I knew was mine and not God's, and feeling, for one ugly second, glad. That second is the sickness. Naming it is the beginning of health.

The charge of 2 Timothy 4 does not lighten as a man grows older in ministry. It grows heavier, because the years add up to a longer list of sermons he will answer for. Paul wrote it from a cell, weeks from execution, with nothing left to gain and nothing left to protect, which is exactly why it is so clean. A man with nothing to protect tells the truth. The truth is that the pulpit is not a stage you have earned. It is a command you have been handed.

Preach the word.

Not because it works. Not because it fills the room. Because you were told to, by a dying man who was told by a risen one, and the judgment seat is real.
chapters.verdict: The pulpit is not yours to fill. It is yours to obey.
reflect: When did you last feel the weight of the charge rather than the pressure of the room?
What are you preaching that you could not defend before God and the living and the dead?
If preaching is obedience before it is art, what would change in how you prepare?

chapters.title: When the People Wept at the Reading
chapters.summary: Nehemiah 8 shows the pattern that founds all expository preaching: the text read clearly, explained faithfully, and the people responding to God rather than to the speaker. The model is older than the church.
chapters.body:
Before there was a sermon there was a reading, and the reading made grown men weep. It is one of the most exact pictures of expository preaching anywhere in Scripture, and it sits in a book most Christians skim, in a chapter about a wall. Nehemiah has rebuilt Jerusalem's defenses. The rubble is cleared. And then, with the work done, the people do something stranger than building: they ask for the book. "And they spake unto Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded to Israel" (Nehemiah 8:1). Notice who initiates. Not the priest. The people. They have been without the word so long that the hunger for it has become a public demand, and they gather as one man in the street before the Water Gate and ask to hear what God said.

What follows is the founding template, and it is so simple that its simplicity is the scandal. Ezra stood on a wooden platform built for the purpose. He opened the book in the sight of all the people, and when he opened it, the people stood. He read from morning until midday. And then comes the sentence that should be carved over the door of every seminary that has ever existed: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Nehemiah 8:8). Read the text. Give the sense. Cause the understanding. That is exposition. That is the whole of it, twenty-five centuries before Robinson wrote *Biblical Preaching* and gave us the vocabulary of the big idea. The Levites did not have his vocabulary. They had his practice.

Look at the order, because the order is the doctrine. First the reading, distinctly. The word comes before the explanation, and it comes whole. There is no sermon yet, only Scripture, read with enough care that the words themselves land. We have nearly lost this. In a great many evangelical services the public reading of Scripture has shrunk to a single verse flashed on a screen, a pretext cleared away in eight seconds so the talking can begin. In Nehemiah the reading lasts hours, and the reading itself is treated as the event. The explanation serves the reading. It does not replace it. A church that will not read the Bible aloud, at length, in the assembly, has already decided that its own commentary is more interesting than its text, and that decision is the seed of everything that goes wrong later.

Then, the giving of the sense. The Hebrew suggests a translating, an opening up, a making plain of what the words mean. The people had been in exile; many spoke Aramaic now; the law needed to be carried across a gap of language and time. This is the work of the expositor exactly. He stands between an ancient text and a present people and he does not invent a bridge of his own design. He carries the meaning that is already there across the distance that has opened up. He gives the sense. He does not impose a sense. There is a universe of difference between explaining what the text says and using the text to say what you had already planned to say, and Nehemiah 8 lands hard on the right side of it. The sense given is the text's own.

And then the result, which is the part no preacher can manufacture. The people wept. They wept at the word, and Nehemiah and Ezra and the Levites had to calm them, telling them the day was holy and they should not mourn but rejoice (Nehemiah 8:9-10). Here is the thing I want every young preacher to see and hold: the weeping was a response to the word, not to the men. Ezra had not told a moving story. He had not built to an emotional crescendo. He had read the law and explained it, and the law itself, understood, broke the people open. Their conviction came from the text. This is the test of whether a sermon has actually been expository. After it is over, are the people responding to God, or to the preacher? Have they met the word, or have they merely admired the man?

Walter Brueggemann argued in *Finally Comes the Poet* that the preacher's task is to speak in a way that lets the holy interrupt our settled prose, that the sermon is the moment a community might be addressed by Another and not merely informed by a peer. Nehemiah 8 is that interruption in its purest form. The people came to hear about a wall, perhaps, or to celebrate a finished project. What met them was the voice of God in his own words, and it leveled them. The poet did not generate the holiness. He let it through. That is the most a preacher can do, and it is enough, and it is everything.

I have learned, slowly and against my instincts, to trust the reading. There were years I treated the Scripture reading in our service as throat-clearing, a thing to get past so I could get to my carefully built remarks. I was wrong, and the wrongness was a kind of unbelief. If I believed the word was living and powerful and sharper than any two-edged sword, I would not have rushed it. I rushed it because somewhere underneath I believed my explanation was the sharp thing and the reading was the dull preliminary. That is the heresy of the modern pulpit stated plainly, and most of us are guilty of it without ever having confessed it as heresy.

Calvin, in Geneva, preached through books of the Bible verse by verse, sometimes returning after an exile to take up the very next verse where he had left off years before, as if the interruption had been a weekend. The continuity was the statement. The text, not the calendar and not the crisis, set the order of his preaching. He trusted that if he simply gave the sense of the next passage, week after week, the whole counsel of God would be delivered to his people without his having to decide which parts they needed. That trust is the spine of the expository method, and it rests on the conviction Nehemiah's people demonstrated: that the book itself is sufficient, that the people are starving for it, and that when it is read distinctly and explained faithfully, God himself addresses the assembly.

The platform Ezra stood on was built of wood and would not have lasted. The pattern he enacted on it has outlasted every empire since. Read the word. Give its sense. Let the understanding come. And then step back, because what happens next is not yours to engineer.

The people wept. They wept because they had heard, at last, the voice they had been built to hear. No preacher gets to take credit for that. Every preacher gets to make room for it, or refuse to.
chapters.verdict: Exposition did not begin as a method. It began as obedience to a recovered book.
reflect: Does your congregation respond to the text, or to you?
What would it mean for your sermon to "give the sense" rather than supply your own?
When did the word last reduce your people to silence or tears?

chapters.title: Two Trades That Wear the Same Robe
chapters.summary: Exposition and topical performance can look identical from the pew, but they answer to different masters. One submits to the text; the other recruits the text to a cause already chosen.
chapters.body:
A man can preach a topical sermon that is more faithful to Scripture than another man's verse-by-verse exposition, and pretending otherwise is how the expository cause makes itself ridiculous. So let me say the hard thing first, against my own team. The form is not the virtue. A preacher can march straight through a book of the Bible, paragraph by paragraph, and still be doing the very thing exposition exists to forbid: using the text as a stage from which to deliver his own opinions, dressed in the costume of verse references. The structure is not the safeguard. The submission is.

That said, the two trades are real, and they are different, and the difference matters more than almost anything else a preacher decides. Exposition lets the text set the agenda. Topical performance brings an agenda and goes looking for texts. From the pew the two can look identical. Both quote the Bible. Both reach a conclusion. Both may move the room. But they answer to different masters, and over years the master shows.

Here is the test, and it is brutally simple. In a genuinely expository sermon, the main point of the sermon is the main point of the passage. Haddon Robinson built his whole approach in *Biblical Preaching* around this, the discipline of finding what he called the big idea of the text and submitting the entire sermon to it. The preacher does not decide what to talk about. The passage decides, and the preacher's labor is to discover that decision and obey it. In a topical performance the preacher decides first, then assembles texts that support the verdict already reached. The texts are witnesses called by the prosecution. They are not permitted to testify against the case.

I want to be careful, because there is an honest topical preaching that the expository tradition has no quarrel with. When a congregation faces a particular crisis, when a doctrine must be taught in its fullness across the whole canon, when a man preaches on marriage or money or suffering and gathers the Scriptures that speak to it, he can do this in submission to the texts he gathers, letting each one say what it says and refusing to make it say more. That is topical method under expository discipline, and the best preachers move between book studies and topical series without ever loosening their grip on the principle. Lloyd-Jones, who is sometimes claimed as a pure verse-by-verse man, in fact preached topically when the occasion called for it, and preached it well, because his submission did not depend on his structure.

The corruption is not topicality. The corruption is the reversal of authority. The corruption is the sermon in which the preacher's point is the master and the Bible is the servant, summoned to lend its dignity to a conclusion the preacher would have reached without it. You can hear the reversal if you listen for it. The proof-text that does not actually say what the preacher claims it says. The verse lifted clean out of its paragraph and made to stand for something its own context contradicts. The relentless return, in every sermon by a particular man, to the same three or four themes regardless of what the passage in front of him is about. That last one is the tell. When a preacher's text changes every week but his sermon never does, he is not expositing anything. He is broadcasting himself on a Scriptural frequency.

I have done this. I have a handful of ideas I love, convictions I came to hard and hold dear, and there were years when every passage I touched somehow arrived at one of them. I told myself this was integration, the connecting of theology to life that I believe in. It was not integration. It was a leash. I had the text on a leash and I was walking it toward my own backyard, and a discerning member of my church told me so, gently, after about the fortieth sermon that ended where the last thirty-nine had ended. He was right. The text was not setting my agenda. My agenda was using the text for cover.

Augustine, in *On Christian Doctrine*, warned against the man who twists obscure passages to support a meaning he favors, and noted that even when the favored meaning is true, the method that arrives at it through abuse of the text is corrupt and trains the hearer in a corrupt way of reading. This is the long damage of topical performance, the damage that outlives any single sermon. It teaches a congregation that the Bible is a quarry for whatever building you have already decided to build. It teaches them that meaning is something you bring to a text rather than something you receive from it. And a congregation trained that way cannot read its own Bible, because it has only ever seen the Bible used and never seen it obeyed. The expository preacher, week after week, is teaching his people how to read, not only what to think. He is modeling submission to a text they will one day open alone.

There is a deeper issue underneath the method, and it is a question about God. The topical performer, at the level of his working assumptions, believes that he knows what his people need and that his job is to deliver it persuasively. The expositor believes that God knows what the people need and has already said it, and that his job is to get out of the way of the saying. One trusts his own diagnosis. The other trusts the Physician. Calvin's confidence in preaching straight through the books of Scripture rested on this exact trust, that the Spirit who inspired the order of the canon would feed the people through it better than the preacher's own sense of the week's most pressing topic ever could. That is not anti-intellectualism. It is a particular intellectual humility, the humility that says my reading of my people's need is fallible, and the word is not.

The two trades wear the same robe. They stand in the same place, hold the same book, use the same vocabulary. But one of them has handed the leash to God, and the other is still holding it, and over a decade in one pulpit the truth comes out. A topical performer's congregation knows the preacher very well. An expositor's congregation knows the Bible. Ask which one a man is by asking what his people have learned to love. If they have learned to love him, examine the trade. If they have learned to love the word, you have your answer, and so does he.

I would rather a congregation forget me entirely and carry the text out the door. The temptation runs the other way, every Sunday. I feel it still. The leash is always in reach.
chapters.verdict: The difference is not the subject. It is who holds the leash.
reflect: Did this week's text choose your subject, or did your subject choose its proof-texts?
Could a hearer reconstruct the passage from your sermon, or only your point?
What does your habitual sermon shape reveal about who you are actually serving?

chapters.title: The Discipline of Letting the Text Win
chapters.summary: Submitting to the text means letting it preach against the preacher's plans, preferences, and prepared conclusions. It is a discipline of surrender practiced in the study before it is seen in the pulpit.
chapters.body:
The first sign that a man is actually doing expository work is that the text starts to ruin his plans. Not occasionally. Routinely. He sits down on Monday with a sense of where the passage is going, where he would like it to go, and somewhere in the labor of study the passage turns and says something he did not want it to say, refuses to make the point he had hoped to make, insists on a meaning that cuts against the very application he had penciled in. And in that moment the whole question of his ministry is decided in private, where no one can see it. Does he let the text win, or does he overrule it?

Most of the corruption of the modern pulpit is not committed in public. It is committed on Tuesday, alone, when a man decides that the text's actual meaning is less useful than the meaning he prefers, and quietly substitutes. The congregation never sees the substitution. They only see a confident man with a Bible. But heaven saw it, and the man's own soul saw it, and over years the habit of overruling the text in the study becomes the inability to hear it at all.

Letting the text win is a discipline, which means it is unnatural and must be practiced against the grain. The grain runs toward self. I open a passage and my mind, trained by years of wanting to be useful and admired, immediately begins scanning it for the sermon I can build. I am not reading. I am mining. And mining is not reading. The first labor of exposition is to stop the mining long enough to actually hear what the passage says on its own terms, in its own context, doing its own work in its own book, before I have any business asking what it means for Tuesday afternoon. Robinson's discipline of the big idea is precisely an instrument for this surrender. By forcing myself to state, in one sentence, what this passage is actually about, I am forbidding myself the luxury of preaching what I wish it were about.

There is a passage I avoided for years. I will not pretend I avoided it by accident. It indicts a thing I do, names a sin I am comfortable with, and every time the preaching calendar drifted toward it I found a reason to take a different text. I told myself I was being strategic. I was being cowardly. The discipline of letting the text win includes the discipline of preaching the texts that win against you, the ones that leave you exposed in your own pulpit, the ones where the honest sermon ends with the preacher inside the indictment rather than above it. Bonhoeffer understood this cost. He wrote about cheap grace from a country that was busy buying it, and the writing cost him everything precisely because he refused to soften the text to fit the moment. The text won. It won at the price of his life. Most of us are not asked to pay that. We are asked only to pay the small price of being wrong in front of our people, of saying out loud that the passage corrects the very thing we had been teaching, and most of us will not pay even that.

Calvin, preaching through Scripture in unbroken sequence, built the surrender into his method structurally. By committing to the next passage in the book, he removed from himself the weekly temptation to choose a text that suited his mood or his agenda. He could not skip the hard verse. It was simply next. Lloyd-Jones, too, in *Preaching and Preachers*, warned against the preacher who is always seeking a striking text, the man hunting for the verse that will let him say the clever thing, and commended instead the man who submits to the discipline of working through Scripture and lets the difficult and the dull and the dangerous passages have their turn. There is wisdom in a method that takes the choosing out of your hands, because the choosing is exactly where self-interest enters.

But the structure alone will not save you, because you can preach in sequence and still overrule the text quietly within each passage. The deeper discipline is interior, and it is this: a settled willingness to be corrected by the word you are preaching. The expositor must come to the text as a hearer before he is a herald. He must be willing to be preached at by the passage before he presumes to preach from it. If a man stands up to deliver a word that has not first done its work on him, he is delivering a corpse, and the people can smell it. They cannot always name what is wrong, but they know. A sermon that has cost the preacher nothing rarely costs the hearer anything either. The text that has not won against the preacher will not win against the pew.

This is why the study is the real battlefield, not the pulpit. By the time a man stands up on Sunday, the war is over. It was fought on Wednesday, over a commentary and a cold cup of coffee, in the moment he saw clearly what the text meant and felt the pull to make it mean something easier. Stott described the preacher's study as a place of wrestling, where the meaning is fought for and the application is hammered out under the pressure of the text's actual demand. The wrestling is the work. The man who skips the wrestling and goes straight to the outline has not prepared a sermon. He has prepared a speech and attached a verse to it.

Let me name the verdict that the discipline serves. The goal is not that the preacher should appear humble. Humility that is performed is just another self-display. The goal is that God should actually be heard, and God cannot be heard through a man who is busy editing him. Every time the preacher overrules the text, he inserts himself between God and the people, and the people go home having heard the preacher's preferences in the costume of God's word, which is worse than hearing nothing, because it inoculates them against the real thing. They think they have heard God. They have heard a man who would not let God win.

I keep a private measure now, and I offer it to you. When I finish studying a passage, I ask whether it has changed anything I planned to say, or whether it has merely confirmed it. If it has only confirmed me, I am suspicious. Not certain I am wrong, but suspicious, because the living word is sharper than that, and a text that only ever agrees with the preacher is probably not being heard at all. It is being used. The texts that change my sermon are the texts I have actually read.

A passage you have never let defeat you is a passage you have never preached. You have only borrowed it. And borrowed words, however eloquent, carry no authority, because authority belongs to the One whose word it is, and he does not lend it to men who will not first obey it themselves.

Let the text win. Lose to it on Tuesday, in private, so that on Sunday the people might win something that will outlast you.
chapters.verdict: A text you have never let defeat you is a text you have never actually preached.
reflect: When did a passage last force you to abandon the sermon you wanted to give?
What in Scripture are you quietly avoiding because it preaches against you?
Is your study a search for the text's meaning, or for your sermon's permission?

chapters.title: The Idol Called Relevance
chapters.summary: The pursuit of relevance, pressed too far, hollows out the pulpit by making the preacher's perceived usefulness the measure of the word. The text is most relevant precisely when it refuses to flatter the moment.
chapters.body:
The most dangerous word in the working vocabulary of the modern pastor is relevance, and it is dangerous precisely because it sounds like love. Of course I want the word to connect. Of course I want it to reach the skeptic in the back row, the exhausted father, the woman whose faith is hanging by a thread. I came to Christ out of atheism, and I remember sitting in a service where the preacher was so determined to be relevant to someone like me that he never actually said anything I could not have read in a self-help paperback. He was reaching for me. He missed, because he had emptied his hands of the only thing I had come, without knowing it, to hear.

Relevance becomes an idol the moment it becomes the measure. As long as relevance is a servant of the text, helping the preacher carry an ancient meaning across the distance to a present hearer, it is honorable work, the bridge-building Stott described. But the idol inverts the relationship. The idol makes the present moment the judge of the word, so that whatever in Scripture seems immediately useful is amplified and whatever seems strange, slow, or offensive is quietly set aside. The preacher begins to edit the canon by the standard of the contemporary, and the standard of the contemporary is, by definition, the thing that does not need the church to survive. We end up preaching the parts of the Bible the world already half-agrees with and burying the parts that would actually disrupt it. We call this meeting people where they are. It is closer to abandoning them there.

Brueggemann, in *Finally Comes the Poet*, made an argument that cuts directly against the relevance idol. He said the dominant consciousness, the settled prose of the culture, is precisely what the prophetic word must interrupt, and that the preacher who only confirms the assumptions his hearers already hold has betrayed the office. The poet, the prophet, the preacher speaks a word from outside the closed system. The relevance idol locks the preacher inside the system and lets the system set the terms. It tells him to speak only in the categories his hearers already accept, about only the problems they already feel, toward only the solutions they already want. But the gospel was never relevant in that sense. The cross was a scandal to the Jew and folly to the Greek (1 Corinthians 1:23), relevant to neither, and Paul refused to file off its edges to make it palatable. He did not preach a Christ adjusted for the audience. He preached Christ crucified, and let the offense stand.

Here is what the relevance idol cannot see: the word is most relevant precisely when it refuses to flatter the moment. The skeptic in the back row does not need a preacher who agrees with him. He needs a word large enough to be worth disbelieving, a claim with enough weight to be worth the argument. When I was an atheist, the Christians who made me think were not the ones who tried to meet me on my own ground. They were the ones who stood on different ground entirely and described it so clearly that I could see it was solid. Their refusal to chase me was the most respectful thing they did. It told me they believed there was somewhere to stand that was not where I was standing. The chasing preacher tells the skeptic, in effect, that there is nowhere to go, only the same anxious ground rearranged. No one crosses an ocean to reach a country identical to the one they left.

The idol exacts a price, and the price is the slow emptying of the pulpit. It happens by degrees. First the hard doctrines go, judgment and wrath and hell and the exclusivity of Christ, because they do not test well. Then the slow texts go, the genealogies and the laws and the long arguments of Romans, because they do not hold attention. Then the strange texts go, the apocalyptic and the imprecatory and the parts that resist a clean application. What remains is a thin band of Scripture, the encouraging and the practical and the inoffensive, preached over and over, and the congregation slowly forgets that the rest of the book exists. They are not being fed the whole counsel of God. They are being fed the relevant fraction, and the relevant fraction cannot sustain a soul through a real catastrophe, because real catastrophes are the moments the relevant fraction never prepared anyone to face.

I have watched this happen in churches I love, and I have felt the pull in my own ministry, the steady gravitational drag toward the useful and away from the true when the two seem to diverge. They do not actually diverge, but they appear to, and the appearance is enough to bend a man over time. The relevance idol whispers that this text, this Sunday, will not land, that the people are tired, that they need something they can use. And the whisper is half true, which is what makes it dangerous. The people are tired. They do need help. But the help they need is not a smaller word. It is the real one, preached into the actual weight of their actual lives, which is a different thing entirely from a word shrunk to fit the size of their attention.

Lloyd-Jones argued that the cure for a powerless church was never a new technique but a recovery of the truth preached with the unction of the Spirit. He was deeply suspicious of every effort to make preaching more effective by making it less theological, because he saw, rightly, that the power was never in the relevance. The power was in the word, applied by the Spirit, and the relevance idol substitutes a human effort for a divine action. It is, at bottom, a failure of faith. It does not believe the word is living and active. It believes the word needs the preacher's cleverage to come alive, and so it pours its energy into the leverage and starves the word.

The verdict is hard, so I will say it plainly and stand under it myself. A pulpit that chases the present forfeits the only thing the present cannot supply. The world is already drowning in relevance. Every screen, every feed, every advertisement is relevant, tuned with terrifying precision to the desires of the moment. If the church offers only more of the same, more relevance, better-targeted, it has nothing. The one thing the church has that the world cannot manufacture is a word from outside the moment, eternal, unbought, indifferent to the algorithms, spoken by a God who was here before the present and will be here after it. That word is the church's only treasure. The relevance idol asks the church to bury its treasure and dig up the world's, and then wonders why the world is not impressed.

I am not against connection. I labor for it. But I have learned to suspect myself most at the exact moment I am most determined to be relevant, because that is the moment I am most tempted to make myself the bridge's destination rather than its span. The destination was never me. It was never the moment. It was the word, and the God who speaks it, and the present has no power to judge what does not belong to it.

Preach what does not need the present's permission. It is the only thing the present cannot give them, and the only thing they cannot live without.
chapters.verdict: A pulpit that chases the present forfeits the only thing the present cannot supply.
reflect: Are you making the word relevant, or trusting that it already is?
What have you stopped preaching because it no longer seemed to "connect"?
Whose approval are you actually seeking when you reach for relevance?

chapters.title: The Cost of the Study
chapters.summary: Faithful exposition demands hours of unglamorous labor in the original meaning, the context, and the structure of the text, work no congregation ever sees but every congregation feels the absence of.
chapters.body:
Every faithful sermon is sitting on top of hours that no one will ever see, and the temptation of ministry is to skip them, because they are invisible and unrewarded and the sermon will happen with or without them. This is the secret arithmetic of the pulpit. A man can stand up unprepared and still fill the time, still hold the room, still receive the handshakes at the door. The cost of the skipped study is not paid on Sunday. It is paid slowly, over years, by a congregation that is being fed thinner and thinner gruel by a preacher who has learned he can get away with it.

The study is unglamorous in a way that nothing else in ministry is. Counseling has its visible fruit. Leadership has its visible influence. Even prayer, done in public, has its witnesses. But the hours a preacher spends alone with a text, tracing an argument through a chapter of Romans, comparing the way a word is used across a Gospel, sitting with a commentary until the structure of a passage finally clicks into place, those hours have no audience and no immediate reward. They are the least visible labor in the pastor's week and the most important, and that combination is exactly why they are the first thing sacrificed when the week gets crowded. Something must give, the man tells himself, and the meeting cannot be moved and the visit cannot be canceled, so the study contracts. He will rely on what he already knows. He will lean on his gifts. He has gotten away with it before.

I have done this, and I want to describe the particular dishonesty of it, because naming the mechanism is the only defense against it. When I shortchange the study, I do not experience myself as lazy. I experience myself as busy, as faithful, as a man so devoted to his people that he is pouring himself out for them in a dozen visible ways. The neglect of the text hides inside the appearance of devotion. I am working hard. I am simply working hard at everything except the one thing the office most requires. And the congregation, on the receiving end, gets a man who is present everywhere except in the word, which is the one place they cannot follow him and so cannot supply for themselves.

The work itself is specific, and it is worth naming, because vagueness about the labor is how the labor gets avoided. The expositor must establish what the text actually says, which means attending to the original where he is able, or to faithful translations and tools where he is not, never preaching a meaning that rests on a translation quirk the original would not support. He must establish the context, the paragraph and the chapter and the book, because a verse torn from its setting can be made to say nearly anything, and the man who preaches verses without contexts is the man who eventually preaches anything he likes. He must trace the structure, the flow of the argument, the way the passage moves from its beginning to its end, because the structure is the author's own emphasis, and to preach against the structure is to preach against the meaning. This is the work Robinson systematized and Stott described and Calvin simply did, week after week, year after year, until the people of Geneva knew their Bibles better than the priests who had kept the book from them for centuries.

There is a theological reason the work cannot be skipped, and it is not merely that good study makes good sermons. It is that the word is God's, and to handle God's word carelessly is to handle God carelessly. Paul charged Timothy to study to show himself approved, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). Rightly dividing. The image is of careful, accurate cutting, the work of a craftsman who respects his material. A man who will not do the work of rightly dividing is not merely a poor craftsman. He is a man who does not sufficiently fear the One whose word he is cutting. The carelessness is, underneath, a kind of contempt, however unintended, and the people absorb the contempt even when they cannot name it. They learn from a careless preacher that the Bible is not worth careful handling, and that lesson, taught week after week, is catastrophic.

Augustine, who had been a professional rhetorician before his conversion, understood that the skill of speaking was nothing without the labor of understanding. In *On Christian Doctrine* he insisted that the would-be teacher must first become a diligent student of the Scriptures, must steep himself in them, must do the slow work of learning before he presumes to teach, and that the man who tries to teach what he has not first labored to understand will only spread his own confusion. The eloquence Augustine prized was the overflow of understanding, not a substitute for it. A man can learn to sound understanding without being it, and the relevance idol of the previous chapter is happy to teach him how, but the sounding without the substance is a fraud, and frauds are eventually found out, usually at the worst possible moment, when a real crisis comes and the congregation reaches for a depth the preacher never built.

Here is the cost stated as plainly as I can state it. There is no shortcut to the study that the people will not eventually pay for. The preacher who skips the hours banks them, in a sense, as a debt, and the debt comes due in the spiritual thinness of his people, in their inability to read their own Bibles, in their helplessness when suffering arrives and the easy applications run out. He has been feeding them a diet that cannot sustain a soul through a long night, and the long night always comes. When it comes, they will reach back into everything he taught them, and they will find, or fail to find, the substance he either built or neglected to build in the unseen hours of a hundred ordinary weeks.

I have set my week around the study now, after years of setting it around everything else and squeezing the study into the gaps. The change was a confession. It admitted that I had been treating the most important work as the most expendable, and that the order of my calendar had been quietly preaching a sermon of its own, a sermon about what I actually valued, week after week, more honest than anything I said from the pulpit. A man's calendar does not lie. It shows what he believes the word is worth.

The hours are still invisible. No one sees me trace the argument of a paragraph for the third time, looking for the connection I keep missing. No one applauds the morning spent learning that the passage does not mean what I had assumed. But God sees the study, and the people feel its presence or its absence as surely as a body feels nourishment or starvation, even when it cannot name the cause. The study is love made invisible. It is the labor a man performs for people who will never know he performed it, so that on Sunday they might be handed something true.

Pay the cost in private, or your people will pay it in public, in the hour they most need what you never built.
chapters.verdict: There is no shortcut to the study that the people will not eventually pay for.
reflect: How many of your sermon hours are spent in the text itself versus its delivery?
What have you let crowd out the study, and what did you tell yourself to justify it?
Would your preparation survive being seen by the God you claim to be quoting?

chapters.title: Preaching as an Act of Love
chapters.summary: The deepest motive for expository preaching is not duty or doctrine but love for the people, a love that refuses to feed them anything less than God's own word.
chapters.body:
Underneath all the argument about method there is a question about love, and it is the question that finally divides the faithful preacher from the merely competent one. Why bother with exposition at all? Why pay the cost of the study, refuse the idol of relevance, let the text win against your plans, when easier paths exist that fill the same room and earn the same praise? The answer is not duty, though duty is real. The answer is not doctrine, though doctrine is true. The deepest answer is love, and a particular kind of love, the kind that refuses to feed the people anything less than God's own word because the people are starving for God and nothing else will fill them.

When Jesus restored Peter on the shore after the resurrection, he did not ask Peter about his theology or his rhetorical gifts. He asked, three times, whether Peter loved him, and three times he tied the answer to a command: feed my sheep (John 21:15-17). Feeding. The image is maternal, domestic, unglamorous. It is the work of putting nourishment into mouths that cannot feed themselves, day after day, with no applause, because the ones being fed are too dependent and too hungry to do anything but eat. That is what preaching is, underneath the platform and the microphone. It is feeding. And the love of Christ is the only motive strong enough to keep a man doing it faithfully when the easier paths beckon, because the easier paths feed the preacher's hunger to be admired while leaving the sheep hungry for the only thing that sustains them.

Here is the cruelty I have come to fear most in myself. The desire to be liked is not, on its face, a vicious thing. It feels like warmth. It feels like care. But it is the most reliable corrupter of the pulpit, because it bends every decision toward the soft word over the true one, the comforting half over the difficult whole, the application that flatters over the rebuke that heals. And the bending is invisible to the man doing it, because it disguises itself as kindness. He tells himself he is sparing the people, when in fact he is sparing himself the discomfort of their displeasure. He withholds the hard word and calls it gentleness. It is not gentleness. It is the cruelty of a physician who will not name the disease because the diagnosis is unpleasant to deliver, and who therefore lets the patient die comfortable and uninformed.

Bonhoeffer's indictment of cheap grace was, at its root, an indictment of preachers who loved their congregations too little to tell them the truth. Cheap grace is grace preached without the cross, forgiveness offered without repentance, comfort dispensed without cost, and it is, Bonhoeffer saw, the preferred product of a clergy that wants to be loved more than it wants its people to be saved. The costly word, the word that demands and disrupts and calls for death before resurrection, is the loving word, even when it does not feel loving in the moment of its delivery. The cheap word, the soothing word, the word that never asks anything, is the cruel one, however warmly it is received. We have inverted these, in our era, and called the cruelty kindness and the kindness cruelty, and a whole generation of congregations has been comforted to death.

I have to confess where I have fallen on the wrong side of this. There are sermons I softened. There are members I did not want to lose, donors I did not want to anger, friends I did not want to wound, and the word I preached to them was bent, subtly, toward their comfort and away from their good. I did not experience myself as a coward in those moments. I experienced myself as pastoral, sensitive, wise about timing. Some of that was real. But some of it was fear wearing the robe of love, and the people I was supposedly loving received less than the word God had for them because I was protecting my standing with them. That is the self-implication I cannot escape and will not pretend away. The kindest preacher I know would rather lose your affection than starve your soul, and I have not always been that preacher.

Keller, whose preaching theory has shaped a generation, argued that preaching must always reach the heart, not merely the intellect, and that the way to the heart is not flattery but the gospel applied to the actual idols and fears of the actual hearers. This is love disciplined by truth. It is not the love that tells the people what they want to hear; it is the love that knows them well enough to tell them what their hearts are actually clutching, and then to pry the fingers loose with the only thing strong enough to do it, which is the news of a Savior who loves them more than their idols ever could. That kind of preaching costs the preacher something. It requires him to know his people, to study their hearts as carefully as he studies his text, and to speak into the gap between what they want and what they need with a courage that only love supplies. Fear cannot do it. Only love can say the hard thing and mean it for the hearer's good.

The expository commitment is, finally, a commitment of love, because it is a commitment to give the people God rather than the preacher. When I submit to the text, when I let it set the agenda and refuse to bend it toward my preferences or theirs, I am insisting that my people deserve the actual word of God and not a substitute, however charming the substitute might be. I am saying that they are worth the cost of the study, worth the risk of the offense, worth the loss of my own popularity, because they are God's sheep and not my fans, and sheep need feeding, not flattering. The topical performer who chases relevance and softens the hard texts is, whatever his intentions, loving himself through his people. The expositor who pays the cost and lets the text win is loving the people through his own discomfort. Same robe. Opposite love.

Peterson spent his ministry insisting that the pastor's work is the slow, unspectacular cultivation of souls, that it cannot be rushed or scaled or performed, that it is more like farming than like manufacturing. Preaching, in that vision, is not a performance delivered to a crowd but a meal prepared for a family, and the question is never how the meal played but whether it nourished. A man can cook to impress or cook to feed, and the dishes may look identical, but the love is different and the family knows the difference over years. They know whether they have been fed or merely entertained, whether they have grown or merely been amused, whether the one in the kitchen was serving them or serving himself.

So I come back to the shore, and to the question that will not leave me. Lovest thou me? Feed my sheep. The whole of expository preaching is contained in those two sentences, the love and the feeding bound together so that neither can exist without the other. To love Christ is to feed his people his word. To feed his people his word is to love them more than I love their approval of me. And to withhold the word for the sake of being liked is the cruelest thing a preacher can do, dressed up as the kindest, fooling everyone, including himself, until the day the unfed sheep go looking for food in the famine and find that their shepherd gave them stones, beautifully arranged, and called it bread.

Feed them. It will cost you their occasional displeasure. Withholding the word will cost them their souls, and you the only thing Christ ever asked you to prove you loved him.
chapters.verdict: To withhold the word for the sake of being liked is the cruelest thing a preacher can do.
reflect: Do you preach to be useful to your people or to be admired by them?
Where has the desire to be liked softened a word your people needed sharp?
If preaching is feeding, what have you actually been setting on the table?

chapters.title: Against the Performance of the Self
chapters.summary: The pulpit's oldest temptation is to display the preacher rather than declare the word. Personality, charisma, and gifting can all become forms of theft from the God who is meant to be heard.
chapters.body:
The most respectable sin in ministry is the one the church most reliably rewards, and that is the display of the self. We have built an entire culture around it. We platform the gifted, we promote the charismatic, we build conferences around the men who can hold ten thousand people and we wonder, quietly, why the churches those men leave behind so often collapse when the personality departs. The answer is uncomfortable. The people had been gathering around a man, and when the man was gone there was nothing underneath, because the man had been the foundation all along, and a man is sand.

Self-display is the oldest temptation of the pulpit because the pulpit is the one place in ordinary life where a person is given sustained, undivided attention by a silent and attentive crowd. There is no other setting like it. The actor shares the stage; the politician faces hecklers; the teacher must manage a room that talks back. The preacher alone is granted thirty or forty minutes of reverent silence from people who have come, in theory, to be changed. That arrangement is an almost irresistible invitation to self-worship, and the tragedy is that the better a man's gifts, the more powerful the invitation, because the more the display actually works. The mediocre preacher is protected from this sin by his mediocrity. The gifted preacher walks toward it every Sunday and must fight it every Sunday, and many do not even know there is a fight.

Spurgeon, who could hold a crowd of thousands without amplification, lived in terror of preaching himself. He understood that his gifts were the very thing most likely to destroy him, that the power to move a room is a power that flatters its possessor into thinking the movement is the point. He insisted that the preacher must decrease so that Christ might increase, echoing the Baptist's own confession that he must decrease while Christ increased (John 3:30), and he meant it as a working discipline and not a pious sentiment. The discipline of decrease. The deliberate, repeated choice to remove the self from the center of the sermon so that the word can occupy it. This is brutally hard for a gifted man, because his gifts are constantly volunteering to take the center, and they take it so gracefully that no one objects, least of all the man himself.

I know this temptation from the inside, and I will not pretend to a humility I have not always practiced. There is a particular pleasure in delivering a line that lands, in feeling a room lean in, in sensing that you have them, and that pleasure is a drug, and like every drug it reorganizes the appetites of the one who tastes it. A preacher who has felt that pleasure begins, without deciding to, to write toward it. He builds his sermons around the moments that produce it. He becomes, by slow degrees, a man optimizing for the experience of being powerful in front of people, and he can do this while preaching impeccably orthodox content, which is what makes it so hard to detect. The doctrine is sound. The texts are handled correctly. And underneath, the whole enterprise has quietly become about the man. The word has become his vehicle rather than his master.

Paul saw this clearly and refused it openly. He told the Corinthians that he came to them not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, that he had determined to know nothing among them save Jesus Christ and him crucified, and that his speech and his preaching were deliberately not with enticing words of man's wisdom, so that their faith would rest on the power of God and not on the wisdom of men (1 Corinthians 2:1-5). Read that as the manifesto it is. Paul, who was capable of dazzling rhetoric when he chose, deliberately disarmed himself before the Corinthians, deliberately refused the tools of self-display, because he understood that a faith built on a preacher's brilliance is a faith built on a man, and men fail, and when the man fails the faith fails with him. He wanted their faith anchored to something that would hold when he was gone, and the only thing that holds is God. So he got himself out of the way on purpose, at the cost of looking less impressive than he could have looked.

This is the deep reason exposition matters, beyond all the arguments about method. Exposition is the discipline that structurally subordinates the preacher to the text. When the main point of the sermon is the main point of the passage, the preacher cannot make himself the point, because the point was decided before he arrived. When the text sets the agenda, the preacher's personality is demoted from author to servant. He may still be vivid, may still be eloquent, may still bear the marks of his particular voice, because God made him a particular man and grace does not erase personality. But the personality is now in service to the word rather than the word in service to the personality, and that inversion is the whole battle. Brueggemann's poet is not displaying his own genius; he is letting a word from outside come through him. The poetry serves the interruption. The moment the poet starts admiring his own poetry, the interruption stops, and the people are left admiring the poet, which is exactly the thing that cannot save them.

There is a test I have learned to apply to my own preaching, and I offer it because it has wounded me usefully. After a sermon, I ask what the people went away talking about. If they went away talking about me, about how I said it, about the line that landed, about the way I held the room, then I have to consider that I preached myself, however orthodox my content. If they went away talking about the text, about what God said, about the thing the passage pressed on them, then perhaps, by grace, I got out of the way enough for the word to be heard. The test is not infallible, because people are kind and will praise the man even when the man got out of the way. But it is a useful warning, and the warning I most need, because my flesh will always prefer to be the one remembered.

Lloyd-Jones distinguished between the preacher who has unction, the genuine anointing of the Spirit, and the preacher who has only natural ability dressed up as anointing, and he insisted the two are different in kind and not merely in degree. Natural ability draws attention to itself. Unction draws attention to God. The same words can carry either, which is what makes the distinction so hard to police from the outside, but the fruit differs over time. Where there is unction, people meet God and are changed and the preacher recedes in their memory. Where there is only ability, people meet a remarkable man and are entertained and the man grows in their memory until he eclipses the God he was meant to reveal. The eclipse is the failure. A preacher exists to point past himself, and a finger that draws the eye to the finger has failed at the one thing fingers are for.

The verdict is unsparing, so let it be unsparing. The more the people see the preacher, the less they hear the Lord. There is a fixed economy here; attention spent on the man is attention withdrawn from the word. A preacher cannot magnify himself and Christ in the same breath, because magnification is a zero-sum thing and the eye goes to whatever is largest in the frame. The faithful preacher spends his whole working life making himself smaller in the frame, decreasing on purpose, removing his own fingerprints from the word so that the word can be heard as God's and not his. It is the most counterintuitive labor in ministry, and the culture of the church fights it at every turn, rewarding the very self-display the calling requires us to crucify.

Get out of the way. They did not come to see you, whatever the applause suggests, and the day you forget that is the day you begin to starve the people who trusted you to feed them God.
chapters.verdict: The more the people see the preacher, the less they hear the Lord.
reflect: When people describe your preaching, do they describe you or what you said?
What gift of yours have you allowed to become the point rather than the instrument?
Could you preach a sermon designed to be forgotten so the text would be remembered?

chapters.title: The Whole Counsel and the Hard Texts
chapters.summary: A faithful pulpit must preach the difficult, the offensive, and the neglected portions of Scripture, not only the comfortable ones. Editing the canon is a failure of trust in the God who gave all of it.
chapters.body:
When Paul said goodbye to the Ephesian elders, knowing he would not see them again, he summarized his ministry among them in a single boast, and it is the only boast a preacher is permitted. He said he was pure from the blood of all men, for he had not shunned to declare unto them the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:26-27). The whole counsel. Not the popular fraction. Not the comfortable selection. The whole. And he tied his innocence of their blood to that completeness, which means that to preach only part of the counsel is, in Paul's accounting, to be in some sense responsible for what the unpreached part would have prevented. That is a terrifying thought, and we have largely stopped thinking it.

Every preacher edits the canon, and most of us do it without admitting we are doing it. We do not announce that we have decided to skip the doctrine of hell, or the texts on judgment, or the hard sayings of Jesus about money and family and the cost of discipleship, or the passages that offend the moral consensus of our particular moment. We simply, over time, do not get to them. The preaching calendar drifts, year after year, toward the texts that comfort and away from the texts that confront, and after a decade a congregation has heard the encouraging psalms many times and the imprecatory psalms never, has heard the love of God in a thousand forms and the wrath of God in none, has been told repeatedly that they are accepted and rarely that they must repent. The editing is invisible because it happens by omission, and omission leaves no fingerprints. But the people are shaped by it as surely as they would be shaped by open heresy, perhaps more surely, because they do not know it is happening.

Here is what I have come to believe about the skipped texts: they are preaching a sermon of their own, and it is a sermon about the preacher's actual theology, the one underneath the one he professes. A man who never preaches judgment is teaching his people that judgment does not much matter, whatever his stated doctrine. A man who never preaches the cost of following Christ is teaching that there is no cost, whatever he says about the cross. The canon he actually preaches is his real confession of faith, and it is often quite different from the confession he would sign. We learn what a preacher truly trusts by watching what he is willing to say, and even more by watching what he consistently refuses to say, because the refusals reveal the fears, and the fears reveal the gods.

The hard texts are hard for a reason, and the reason is usually that they cut against something we love. The texts on money are hard because we love money. The texts on sexual purity are hard because we love our autonomy. The texts on judgment are hard because we love a god who never finally says no. The texts on the exclusivity of Christ are hard because we love the approval of a pluralist culture. In every case the difficulty is located not in the text but in us, in our attachment to the very thing the text means to dislodge, and the preacher who avoids the hard text is protecting his people's idols, and his own, under the guise of pastoral sensitivity. He is not sparing them. He is colluding with the thing that is destroying them, because the idol the text would have named goes on unnamed and therefore unchallenged and therefore enthroned.

Bonhoeffer preached in a church that had made a catastrophic set of omissions, that had quietly stopped preaching the texts that would have armed its people against the ideology rising around them, and the cost of those omissions was a church that could not resist when resistance was the whole of faithfulness. The unpreached texts left the people defenseless. When the moment came that required them to stand on a hard word, they had never been given the hard word, and so they fell, in large numbers, with their pastors leading the fall. This is the long-range stakes of the whole counsel, and it is why Paul tied it to innocence of blood. The texts a preacher skips in the comfortable years are precisely the texts his people will need in the catastrophic ones, and the catastrophe always comes, and it always comes for the thing the comfortable preaching never prepared anyone to face.

I have skipped texts. I have looked at a passage coming up in a series and thought, not this month, the church is fragile right now, the timing is wrong, and sometimes the judgment was genuinely pastoral and sometimes it was cowardice wearing pastoral robes, and I have not always been able to tell the difference in the moment, which is exactly the problem. The flesh is endlessly inventive in supplying noble reasons for ignoble avoidances. The only defense I have found is structural, the same defense Calvin used: preach through the books, and let the hard texts arrive in their turn, not because I chose them but because they are simply next, so that my cowardice is denied the opportunity to do its quiet editing. When the hard text is next, I must either preach it or openly skip it, and the openness of the skip exposes it for what it is, where the invisible drift of selective preaching never has to face the light.

There is a theological humility at stake here that I want to name precisely. When I edit the canon, I am claiming to know better than God what my people need. I am overruling his choice of what to include with my sense of what they can handle. But the canon is God's curriculum, assembled under his providence, every part of it given for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works (2 Timothy 3:16-17). All scripture. The furnishing is incomplete without the whole, and the man of God is left half-equipped, missing exactly the tools the comfortable preaching declined to hand him. To trust God's choice of what to include over my sense of what to preach is an act of faith, and the refusal to trust it is, at bottom, the same unbelief that animates every other failure of the pulpit. It does not believe the hard word is for the people's good. It believes the hard word is a danger to be managed, and so it manages it, into silence.

The whole counsel includes the parts that will lose me people. It includes the doctrines that will draw the angry email, the rebukes that will cool a friendship, the claims that will mark me, in my cultural moment, as the wrong kind of person. Paul knew this. He told the Ephesians that grievous wolves would enter and that men would arise speaking perverse things, and his defense against that future was not strategy but completeness, the whole counsel declared in full so that the people would have everything they needed to stand. He did not curate. He delivered all of it, and then he could say his hands were clean. I want to be able to say that. I am not always able to say it, and the gap between Paul's confidence and my hesitation is the measure of the work I still have to do.

The texts you skip are preaching a sermon of their own, and your people are hearing it, and it is teaching them that the parts of God you find inconvenient do not finally matter. That is the most dangerous sermon in any pulpit, and it is preached entirely in silence, by the man who thought his silence was kindness.

Declare the whole of it. The blood of the unprepared is on the hands of the preacher who decided, for their comfort, to give them only half.
chapters.verdict: The texts you skip are preaching a sermon of their own about what you really believe.
reflect: Which portions of Scripture have quietly disappeared from your preaching?
What hard doctrine have you not addressed because you feared the response?
Do you trust God's choice of what to include more than your own sense of what they can handle?

chapters.title: The Preacher Who Is Preached To
chapters.summary: The man who would preach the word must first be addressed by it; a sermon that has not first searched the preacher cannot search the people. Exposition begins with the preacher's own submission to the text.
chapters.body:
There is a question that exposes a preacher more completely than any other, and it is not about his theology or his technique. It is this: when was the last time the word you were preparing to preach to others first preached to you? Not informed you. Not supplied you. Preached to you, searched you, found you out, left you on your knees before you stood at the desk to build the outline. If the answer is that you cannot remember, then whatever you are doing on Sundays, you are not preaching in the full sense, because the word that has not first done its work on the herald cannot do its work through him.

The preacher is, before anything else, a hearer. This is the order Scripture insists on and the order the office most easily forgets. James warned that not many should become teachers, knowing that they would receive the greater judgment (James 3:1), and the greater judgment falls precisely here, on the man who handles the word professionally and ceases to be addressed by it personally. There is no more dangerous position in the church than the position of a man who has learned to study the Bible only for others, who opens it always with a sermon in mind and never with his own soul exposed, who has become a pipe through which the water flows without ever drinking. The pipe stays dry while everything passes through it. That is the occupational disease of the pulpit, and it is nearly invisible, because the man is constantly in the word and constantly speaking it, and who would suspect that the man most surrounded by Scripture might be the man least nourished by it?

I have lived in the dry pipe, and I want to describe how it happens, because it does not announce itself as backsliding. It happens through faithfulness, oddly enough. A man becomes so diligent in preparing the word for his people that he loses the habit of receiving it for himself. Every reading becomes professional. He cannot open the Psalms without scanning for a series; he cannot read the Gospels without filing illustrations; the text that should be addressing his own heart is intercepted, every time, by the working part of his mind that is already building Sunday. The very diligence that makes him a good craftsman makes him a starving man, because he has forgotten how to come to the word with empty hands, asking nothing for anyone else, only to be met by God himself. The cure is not less study. The cure is a separate hearing, a place where he comes to the word not as a preacher but as a sheep, and lets it feed him before he carries it to the rest of the flock.

Bonhoeffer, who trained pastors in an illegal seminary while his country descended into evil, built that training around the daily, personal hearing of the word, the meditation on Scripture not for sermon material but for the soul, the discipline of letting the text address the man before the man ever addressed a congregation. He understood that a pastor formed only by his professional handling of Scripture would be hollow, and that hollow men cannot stand in the hour of testing. The personal hearing was the foundation. Everything public rested on it, and where it was missing, the public ministry was a shell waiting to crack. He proved the point with his life. The men who stood were the men the word had first searched in private; the men who fell were, so often, the men who had only ever used it in public.

The principle has a hard edge, and the edge cuts toward authenticity of a kind I am permitted to name even when the word for it is forbidden. A preacher can only deliver a word with power to the degree that the word has had power over him. When I preach repentance from a heart that is itself repenting, the people feel the difference, even when they cannot name it. When I preach repentance as a topic I have mastered, having myself repented of nothing lately, the words are correct and the room is dead, and I go home wondering why the sermon did not land when the exegesis was sound. The exegesis was sound. The preacher was hollow. The word had not had its way with me, and so it could not have its way through me, because the Spirit who applies the word to the hearers is the same Spirit who must first apply it to the herald, and he will not be hurried past the herald to get to the flock.

Lloyd-Jones spoke of preaching as logic on fire, theology coming through a man who is aflame, and the fire is exactly this: the word having so gripped the preacher that it comes out of him hot, carrying the heat of its own work in his soul. A man cannot fake the fire. He can fake passion, can raise his voice and quicken his pace and manufacture the appearance of intensity, but the manufactured fire is cold underneath and the people feel the cold. The real fire is lit in the study and in the prayer closet, when the text catches the preacher himself, when the thing he is about to preach to others first burns through his own defenses and leaves him changed. That fire cannot be scheduled. It can only be sought, in the posture of a hearer, by a man humble enough to be preached to before he presumes to preach.

There is a deep mercy in this arrangement, and I want to end on it rather than on the warning. God will not let the preacher escape the word. He will not permit the herald to remain forever outside the message, dispensing a grace he has never received, naming sins he has never confessed, offering a Savior he has kept at professional distance. The very texts the preacher studies will, if he lets them, turn and search him, and the searching is a kindness, because it keeps him a Christian and not merely a clergyman. The man who is preached to as he prepares to preach is being pastored by the same word he is preparing to pastor others with, fed at the same table he is setting, and that double work of the word, on the herald and then through him, is one of the quiet graces of the office that makes the loneliness of the study bearable. He is not alone in there. He is being met.

Peterson resisted, his whole ministry long, the reduction of the pastor to a religious professional, a manager of spiritual goods, and insisted instead that the pastor must remain a person under the word, formed by it, addressed by it, kept small by it. He saw that the professionalizing of ministry was a way of escaping the word's authority while appearing to serve it, of handling the holy without being burned by it. The remedy was to stay a hearer, to refuse the distance that expertise offers, to come to the Bible always as one who needs it and not merely as one who dispenses it. That refusal is a daily discipline and a lifelong one, and the men who keep it are the men whose preaching stays alive into old age, while the men who lose it become, by degrees, eloquent corpses, technically proficient and spiritually dead, preaching a word that no longer touches them and therefore can no longer touch anyone.

You cannot hand the people a word that has never had its way with you. You can hand them the words, correctly arranged, accurately exegeted, beautifully delivered, and they will go home hungry, because words are not the word, and the word comes only through a man it has first laid hold of. Be laid hold of first. Be the preacher who is preached to, every week, before you climb the stairs. Then climb them, carrying not a lecture you have prepared but a fire you have caught, and let it spread.
chapters.verdict: You cannot hand the people a word that has never had its way with you.
reflect: Has the sermon you are preparing convicted you before it convicts them?
When did Scripture last change you rather than merely supply you?
Are you a herald of a word that owns you, or a vendor of words you have never obeyed?

chapters.title: A Word That Outlasts the Voice
chapters.summary: The preacher's labor is to deliver something that will hold after he is gone; the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of God endures forever. Faithful exposition builds on the only foundation that survives.
chapters.body:
Every preacher is building something that will outlast him, or failing to, and the question of which one is decided not at the end but in the daily choice of what to put at the center of the sermon. A ministry built on a man ends when the man ends. A ministry built on the word endures, because the word endures, and the only way to build on the word is to preach it, week after week, in submission, refusing every easier foundation that the sand of personality and relevance and applause is constantly offering. This is the final argument for expository preaching, and it is an argument about time, about what survives, about what a preacher leaves behind when the voice that thrilled the room has fallen silent forever.

Isaiah saw it. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth, because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it; surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever (Isaiah 40:6-8). The preacher is grass. His gifts are grass. His charisma, his reputation, his ability to fill a room, all of it is grass, and the wind of God is already blowing on it, and it is already fading, though he cannot feel the fading in the years of his strength. The word alone stands. And the only ministry that stands is the ministry that bound itself to the word, that made the standing thing its foundation rather than the fading thing, that built its house on the rock of what God said rather than the sand of who the preacher was. Peter quotes this very passage and then adds the line that turns it toward us: this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you (1 Peter 1:25). The enduring word is the preached word. The thing that lasts forever is the very thing the preacher holds in his hands on Sunday morning.

I have buried members of my congregation, and I have learned at gravesides what I could not learn in the comfort of the study. At a graveside the preacher's eloquence is worth exactly nothing. The grieving do not need a clever man; they need a word from outside the grave, a word that the grave cannot touch, and the only such word is the word of God. I have stood at the edge of holes in the ground and watched people reach back for whatever they had been given over the years, and I have seen the difference, stark and unmistakable, between those who had been fed the word and those who had been fed the preacher.
