The ones who had only the preacher had nothing at the graveside, because the preacher's charm does not reach into a casket. The ones who had the word had something to stand on, because the word of God reaches places no human voice can follow, into the ground and past it. That is the moment the whole argument of this book comes due. That is when you learn what you actually built.

Bonhoeffer was hanged at Flossenbürg in April 1945, days before the camp was liberated, and the witnesses said he went to the gallows composed, having just led a final service. What held him in that hour was not his theology as an achievement but the word as a possession, the Scripture he had heard and obeyed and let search him for years, returning to him at the end as the only thing strong enough to face the rope. The word he had preached to others held him when nothing else could, because he had not merely studied it but submitted to it, had let it become the foundation rather than the material. His books endure, yes, but what endured in the moment of his death was the word itself, the thing he had bound his life to, standing for him when everything else had been stripped away. That is the test no preacher can dodge forever, and it is the test the comfortable seasons of ministry are quietly preparing us either to pass or to fail.

What we are doing, in the unglamorous labor of expository preaching, is depositing the enduring word into people who will need it at the hour when nothing else will serve. We are building, in them, a foundation we will not be present to defend, equipping them for catastrophes we will not witness, putting into their hands a word that will speak after our own voices have fallen silent. This is the long obedience of the pulpit, and it does not look like much in any given week. A man stands up, opens a text, gives its sense, sits down. The room half-listens. Nothing visibly changes. But over the years, sermon by sermon, the word is being deposited, and the deposit is the thing that lasts, and one day, in a hospital room or a graveside or a midnight of the soul, the deposit will be drawn upon by a person the preacher may have long forgotten, and the word will be there, standing, when the preacher himself is dust.

So the final discipline is the discipline of building for a time you will not see. It is the willingness to make the sermon about the enduring thing rather than the impressive thing, even when the impressive thing would serve you better in the short term, because the short term is grass and the word is not. It is the choice, repeated across a ministry, to decrease so that the word might increase, to get out of the way so that what survives the preacher might be deposited cleanly, unmixed with the preacher's own fading glory. The man who preaches himself builds a monument that the first strong wind will scatter. The man who preaches the word builds on the rock, and though the building looks plainer and draws smaller crowds and earns less applause, it stands, and it goes on standing after the builder is forgotten, which is exactly as it should be, because the building was never about the builder.

I will be forgotten. This is not false humility; it is arithmetic. Within a generation or two of my death, no one will remember my sermons, my turns of phrase, the way I held a room on a good Sunday. The grass withers. But if I have preached the word, then something will remain that is not me, deposited in people and passed to their children, the enduring word standing in lives I will never know about, doing its work long after my own work has ended. That is the only success the pulpit offers that is worth wanting, and it requires the preacher to want his own forgetting, to labor for an outcome in which he disappears and the word remains. It is the strangest ambition in the world, the ambition to be forgotten so that God might be remembered, and it is the only ambition the office permits.

They will forget your sermons. They will forget your name, eventually, and your face, and the particular gifts you were so tempted to display. The wind is already blowing on the grass, and you are the grass. Make sure, then, that what you hand them is not the grass but the word, the thing that does not wither, the thing that will stand at their gravesides and yours and at the great appearing Paul invoked when he first laid the charge. Preach the word. Build on the only foundation that survives the builder. And then, having built it, be willing to vanish into it, content to be the forgotten herald of a word that will never, world without end, be forgotten.

The grass withers. The word stands. Spend your one life on the thing that lasts.
chapters.verdict: They will forget your sermons. Make sure they cannot forget the word.
reflect: What will remain in your people when you and your voice are gone?
Are you building their faith on the word or on yourself?
If your ministry were measured by what endures, what have you actually built?
